q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'an old flame'
opts: to do things in the wrong order
already decided and unlikely to change
exp: 'an old flame' means 'a former lover' (Hindi: पुराना प्रेमी/प्रेमिका). The other options are the meanings of 'put the cart before the horse'; 'green with envy'; 'cut and dried' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to remember'
opts: By the skin of one's teeth
exp: 'bear in mind' means 'to remember' (Hindi: याद रखना). Others: 'a far cry' = very different from; 'on the cards' = likely to happen; 'by the skin of one's teeth' = only just; narrowly.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'move heaven and earth'
opts: to try every possible means to achieve something
a decisive test of value or quality
exp: 'move heaven and earth' means 'to try every possible means to achieve something' (Hindi: ज़मीन-आसमान एक करना). The other options are the meanings of 'rank and file'; 'an acid test'; 'miss the boat' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to fail or succeed by one's own efforts'
exp: 'sink or swim' means 'to fail or succeed by one's own efforts' (Hindi: अपने बलबूते पर). Others: 'an ivory tower' = a state of isolation from the practical realities of life; 'a snake in the grass' = a hidden enemy; 'pour oil on troubled waters' = to calm a quarrel.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'free and not captured'
exp: 'at large' means 'free and not captured' (Hindi: फ़रार, खुला घूमना). Others: 'out of the blue' = unexpectedly; 'stand one's ground' = to refuse to give way; 'an open secret' = something supposed to be secret but known to all.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'a turncoat'
opts: a person who changes sides or principles
to regret something that cannot be undone
exp: 'a turncoat' means 'a person who changes sides or principles' (Hindi: दलबदलू). The other options are the meanings of 'at loggerheads'; 'cry over spilt milk'; 'grease the palm' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'born with a silver spoon in one's mouth'
opts: to run away quickly and escape
exp: 'born with a silver spoon in one's mouth' means 'born in a rich family' (Hindi: अमीर घर में जन्मा). The other options are the meanings of 'take the bull by the horns'; 'show a clean pair of heels'; 'an old flame' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'pull strings'
opts: to shift responsibility to someone else
exp: 'pull strings' means 'to use one's influence secretly' (Hindi: सिफ़ारिश लगाना, प्रभाव का प्रयोग). The other options are the meanings of 'pass the buck'; 'pour oil on troubled waters'; 'alpha and omega' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'a thorn in the flesh'
exp: 'a thorn in the flesh' means 'a constant source of annoyance' (Hindi: लगातार परेशानी का कारण). The other options are the meanings of 'at the eleventh hour'; 'a Himalayan blunder'; 'a dog's life' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'eat humble pie'
opts: to be dismissed from a job
to apologise humbly; to accept humiliation
exp: 'eat humble pie' means 'to apologise humbly; to accept humiliation' (Hindi: अपमान सहकर माफ़ी माँगना). The other options are the meanings of 'get the sack'; 'keep up appearances'; 'when pigs fly' respectively.

q: Which of the following idioms is CORRECTLY matched with its meaning?
opts: Cast pearls before swine – everyone without distinction
A skeleton in the cupboard – a shameful secret
All and sundry – to try to do more than one is able to
Bite off more than one can chew – to offer something valuable to those who cannot appreciate it
exp: 'a skeleton in the cupboard' means 'a shameful secret' (छिपा हुआ शर्मनाक रहस्य). Correct meanings of the others: 'all and sundry' = everyone without distinction; 'bite off more than one can chew' = to try to do more than one is able to; 'cast pearls before swine' = to offer something valuable to those who cannot appreciate it.

q: Which of the following idioms is NOT correctly matched with its meaning?
opts: Out of sorts – slightly unwell or upset
Have a finger in every pie – to be involved in many activities
A sweet tooth – a liking for sweet food
A rule of thumb – born in a rich family
exp: 'a rule of thumb' means 'a practical method based on experience' (अनुभव पर आधारित नियम), not 'born in a rich family' (that is the meaning of 'born with a silver spoon in one's mouth'). The other pairs are correct.

q: Which of the following idioms is CORRECTLY matched with its meaning?
opts: Lead a dog's life – to live a miserable life
As fit as a fiddle – at a very short distance
At a stone's throw – to stop something at an early stage
Nip in the bud – in very good health
exp: 'lead a dog's life' means 'to live a miserable life' (दयनीय जीवन जीना). Correct meanings of the others: 'nip in the bud' = to stop something at an early stage; 'as fit as a fiddle' = in very good health; 'at a stone's throw' = at a very short distance.

q: Which of the following idioms is CORRECTLY matched with its meaning?
opts: In high spirits – to reverse a situation to one's advantage
Turn the tables – in a straight line
As the crow flies – very cheerful
exp: 'chicken-hearted' means 'cowardly' (कायर, डरपोक). Correct meanings of the others: 'turn the tables' = to reverse a situation to one's advantage; 'as the crow flies' = in a straight line; 'in high spirits' = very cheerful.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to be a common trait in a family'
exp: 'run in the family' means 'to be a common trait in a family' (Hindi: ख़ानदानी गुण होना). Others: 'be all and end all' = the most important part; 'go to the wall' = to be ruined; to fail in business; 'talk shop' = to talk about one's work outside working hours.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'at the last possible moment'
opts: Make a mountain of a molehill
exp: 'at the eleventh hour' means 'at the last possible moment' (Hindi: अंतिम क्षण में). Others: 'a busman's holiday' = a holiday spent doing one's usual work; 'make a mountain of a molehill' = to exaggerate a minor problem; 'a damp squib' = something that turns out to be disappointing.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'uncomfortable or embarrassed'
exp: 'ill at ease' means 'uncomfortable or embarrassed' (Hindi: बेचैन, असहज). Others: 'a narrow escape' = escape from danger with very little margin; 'follow suit' = to do the same as someone else; 'root and branch' = thoroughly, completely.

q: Which of the following idioms is NOT correctly matched with its meaning?
opts: Put the cart before the horse – to do things in the wrong order
Run riot – slightly unwell or upset
A cry in the wilderness – an appeal that nobody listens to
Split hairs – to make unnecessarily fine distinctions
exp: 'run riot' means 'to behave in an uncontrolled way' (उपद्रव मचाना), not 'slightly unwell or upset' (that is the meaning of 'out of sorts'). The other pairs are correct.

q: Which of the following idioms is NOT correctly matched with its meaning?
opts: Dance to someone's tune – the beginning and the end
Make one's blood boil – to make someone very angry
Eat crow – to admit that one was wrong
Smell a rat – to suspect something wrong
exp: 'dance to someone's tune' means 'to obey someone without question' (किसी के इशारों पर नाचना), not 'the beginning and the end' (that is the meaning of 'alpha and omega'). The other pairs are correct.

q: Which of the following idioms is NOT correctly matched with its meaning?
opts: A fly in the ointment – a small flaw that spoils something
Lead a dog's life – to live a miserable life
At daggers drawn – bitterly hostile to each other
On the spur of the moment – to offer something valuable to those who cannot appreciate it
exp: 'on the spur of the moment' means 'suddenly, without planning' (आवेश में, बिना सोचे), not 'to offer something valuable to those who cannot appreciate it' (that is the meaning of 'cast pearls before swine'). The other pairs are correct.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'on the rocks'
opts: to do one's fair share of work
in serious difficulty, likely to fail
to work or study late into the night
exp: 'on the rocks' means 'in serious difficulty, likely to fail' (Hindi: संकट में, टूटने के कगार पर). The other options are the meanings of 'burn the midnight oil'; 'burn one's fingers'; 'pull one's weight' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to forget past quarrels'
exp: 'let bygones be bygones' means 'to forget past quarrels' (Hindi: बीती ताहि बिसार दे). Others: 'in the doldrums' = in low spirits; inactive; 'go haywire' = to go out of control; 'crocodile tears' = false or insincere sorrow.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'a sweet tooth'
opts: to say exactly the right thing
exp: 'a sweet tooth' means 'a liking for sweet food' (Hindi: मिठाई का शौक़). The other options are the meanings of 'hit the nail on the head'; 'dance to someone's tune'; 'a close shave' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to change or disappear very slowly'
exp: 'die hard' means 'to change or disappear very slowly' (Hindi: आसानी से न मिटना). Others: 'read between the lines' = to understand the hidden meaning; 'win hands down' = to win easily; 'put one's foot down' = to take a firm stand.

q:
Match the idioms in List-I with their meanings in List-II:
List-I: (A) An apple of discord; (B) Cast a slur; (C) Run the gauntlet; (D) A herculean task
List-II: (1) a cause of quarrel; (2) a task requiring very great effort; (3) to bring disgrace to; (4) to face criticism or danger from many sides
exp: Correct matching: 'an apple of discord' = a cause of quarrel; 'cast a slur' = to bring disgrace to; 'run the gauntlet' = to face criticism or danger from many sides; 'a herculean task' = a task requiring very great effort. Hence A-1, B-3, C-4, D-2.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'secret, underhand'
exp: 'hole and corner' means 'secret, underhand' (Hindi: गुप्त, चोरी-छिपे). Others: 'an arm and a leg' = a very high price; 'under a cloud' = under suspicion; 'lay down one's arms' = to surrender.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'fight shy of'
exp: 'fight shy of' means 'to avoid' (Hindi: कतराना). The other options are the meanings of 'when pigs fly'; 'a bed of roses'; 'rise like a phoenix' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'play to the gallery'
opts: a decisive test of value or quality
to try to win popular approval
exp: 'play to the gallery' means 'to try to win popular approval' (Hindi: सस्ती लोकप्रियता पाने का प्रयास). The other options are the meanings of 'a far cry'; 'a man of letters'; 'an acid test' respectively.

q: Which of the following idioms is CORRECTLY matched with its meaning?
opts: Have a finger in every pie – to be involved in many activities
In vain – not meant seriously, ironically
Tongue in cheek – a person who can do many kinds of work
A jack of all trades – without success
exp: 'have a finger in every pie' means 'to be involved in many activities' (हर काम में दख़ल देना). Correct meanings of the others: 'tongue in cheek' = not meant seriously, ironically; 'a jack of all trades' = a person who can do many kinds of work; 'in vain' = without success.

q: Which of the following idioms is CORRECTLY matched with its meaning?
opts: Cheek by jowl – to be satisfied with past success and stop trying
A skeleton in the cupboard – very close together
As cool as a cucumber – very calm and composed
Rest on one's laurels – a shameful secret
exp: 'as cool as a cucumber' means 'very calm and composed' (अत्यंत शांत). Correct meanings of the others: 'cheek by jowl' = very close together; 'rest on one's laurels' = to be satisfied with past success and stop trying; 'a skeleton in the cupboard' = a shameful secret.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'apple-pie order'
opts: a state of isolation from the practical realities of life
to be dismissed from a job
exp: 'apple-pie order' means 'perfect order' (Hindi: पूर्ण व्यवस्थित). The other options are the meanings of 'an ivory tower'; 'get the sack'; 'head over heels' respectively.

q:
Match the idioms in List-I with their meanings in List-II:
List-I: (A) A penny for your thoughts; (B) A cock and bull story; (C) Pour oil on troubled waters; (D) A slip of the tongue
List-II: (1) a request to know what someone is thinking; (2) an absurd, unbelievable story; (3) to calm a quarrel; (4) an unintentional error in speaking
exp: Correct matching: 'a penny for your thoughts' = a request to know what someone is thinking; 'a cock and bull story' = an absurd, unbelievable story; 'pour oil on troubled waters' = to calm a quarrel; 'a slip of the tongue' = an unintentional error in speaking. Hence A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'a wet blanket'
opts: a person who spoils the enjoyment of others
exp: 'a wet blanket' means 'a person who spoils the enjoyment of others' (Hindi: रंग में भंग डालने वाला). The other options are the meanings of 'cool one's heels'; 'smell a rat'; 'a bed of roses' respectively.

q:
Match the idioms in List-I with their meanings in List-II:
List-I: (A) Keep up appearances; (B) A man of straw; (C) Upset the apple cart; (D) By fits and starts
List-II: (1) to maintain an outward show; (2) to spoil a plan; (3) a person of no substance or means; (4) irregularly; not continuously
exp: Correct matching: 'keep up appearances' = to maintain an outward show; 'a man of straw' = a person of no substance or means; 'upset the apple cart' = to spoil a plan; 'by fits and starts' = irregularly; not continuously. Hence A-1, B-3, C-2, D-4.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to decide'
exp: 'make up one's mind' means 'to decide' (Hindi: निर्णय करना). Others: 'the talk of the town' = a person or thing everyone is talking about; 'a red letter day' = a memorable or important day; 'get into hot water' = to get into trouble.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'under all circumstances'
exp: 'through thick and thin' means 'under all circumstances' (Hindi: हर परिस्थिति में). Others: 'blow hot and cold' = to keep changing one's opinion; 'on the rocks' = in serious difficulty, likely to fail; 'out of the wood' = out of danger or difficulty.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'get cold feet'
opts: to become nervous and lose courage
exp: 'get cold feet' means 'to become nervous and lose courage' (Hindi: डर से पीछे हटना). The other options are the meanings of 'read between the lines'; 'blue blood'; 'in the long run' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'a hidden enemy'
exp: 'a snake in the grass' means 'a hidden enemy' (Hindi: छिपा हुआ शत्रु). Others: 'bag and baggage' = with all one's belongings; 'chicken-hearted' = cowardly; 'an ivory tower' = a state of isolation from the practical realities of life.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'off the cuff'
opts: a bribe to quieten a troublesome person
exp: 'off the cuff' means 'without preparation' (Hindi: बिना तैयारी के). The other options are the meanings of 'a sop to Cerberus'; 'at daggers drawn'; 'in the doldrums' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'in the bad books'
opts: to escape from danger or punishment
exp: 'in the bad books' means 'out of favour' (Hindi: किसी की नज़र में बुरा). The other options are the meanings of 'save one's skin'; 'see the light'; 'carry the day' respectively.

q: Which of the following idioms is CORRECTLY matched with its meaning?
opts: Once in a blue moon – a very small amount compared with what is needed
A drop in the ocean – a full and satisfying meal
A bad egg – a worthless or dishonest person
exp: 'a bad egg' means 'a worthless or dishonest person' (बुरा आदमी). Correct meanings of the others: 'a drop in the ocean' = a very small amount compared with what is needed; 'a square meal' = a full and satisfying meal; 'once in a blue moon' = very rarely.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'a person of great worth'
exp: 'salt of the earth' means 'a person of great worth' (Hindi: अत्यंत भला व्यक्ति). Others: 'cry for the moon' = to ask for something impossible; 'rise to the occasion' = to deal successfully with a difficult situation; 'burn one's fingers' = to suffer loss through meddling.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'blue blood'
exp: 'blue blood' means 'of noble birth' (Hindi: कुलीन वंश). The other options are the meanings of 'fall out'; 'be all and end all'; 'give and take' respectively.

q: Which of the following idioms is NOT correctly matched with its meaning?
opts: A fly in the ointment – a small flaw that spoils something
Cry over spilt milk – to regret something that cannot be undone
An armchair critic – completely extinct or out of date
Cheek by jowl – very close together
exp: 'an armchair critic' means 'one who criticises without practical experience' (बिना अनुभव का आलोचक), not 'completely extinct or out of date' (that is the meaning of 'as dead as a dodo'). The other pairs are correct.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'nip in the bud'
opts: to stop something at an early stage
to offer something valuable to those who cannot appreciate it
exp: 'nip in the bud' means 'to stop something at an early stage' (Hindi: शुरुआत में ही ख़त्म करना). The other options are the meanings of 'at the helm of affairs'; 'show the white feather'; 'cast pearls before swine' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'do away with'
exp: 'do away with' means 'to abolish' (Hindi: समाप्त करना). The other options are the meanings of 'few and far between'; 'under the weather'; 'drive home' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'call the shots'
opts: to treat someone with deliberate coldness
to be in charge and make decisions
exp: 'call the shots' means 'to be in charge and make decisions' (Hindi: निर्णय लेने का अधिकार रखना). The other options are the meanings of 'take to task'; 'hole and corner'; 'give the cold shoulder' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'an armchair critic'
opts: one who criticises without practical experience
exp: 'an armchair critic' means 'one who criticises without practical experience' (Hindi: बिना अनुभव का आलोचक). The other options are the meanings of 'in the doldrums'; 'an Achilles' heel'; 'all thumbs' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'likely to happen'
exp: 'on the cards' means 'likely to happen' (Hindi: संभावित). Others: 'gain ground' = to make progress; to become more popular; 'a flash in the pan' = a sudden success that is not repeated; 'on the rocks' = in serious difficulty, likely to fail.

q: Which of the following idioms is CORRECTLY matched with its meaning?
opts: A pretty kettle of fish – very calm and composed
A moot point – a debatable question
A gift of the gab – an awkward or difficult situation
As cool as a cucumber – the ability to speak fluently and persuasively
exp: 'a moot point' means 'a debatable question' (विवादास्पद विषय). Correct meanings of the others: 'a gift of the gab' = the ability to speak fluently and persuasively; 'a pretty kettle of fish' = an awkward or difficult situation; 'as cool as a cucumber' = very calm and composed.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'a person who can do many kinds of work'
exp: 'a jack of all trades' means 'a person who can do many kinds of work' (Hindi: हरफ़नमौला). Others: 'by fits and starts' = irregularly; not continuously; 'a leap in the dark' = an action whose result cannot be foreseen; 'cool one's heels' = to be kept waiting.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to show one's feelings openly'
opts: Wear one's heart on one's sleeve
exp: 'wear one's heart on one's sleeve' means 'to show one's feelings openly' (Hindi: भावनाएँ खुलकर प्रकट करना). Others: 'throw in the towel' = to admit defeat; 'turn a deaf ear' = to refuse to listen; 'a leap in the dark' = an action whose result cannot be foreseen.

q: Which of the following idioms is CORRECTLY matched with its meaning?
opts: An acid test – just in time
Blow hot and cold – a decisive test of value or quality
In the teeth of – in spite of strong opposition
In the nick of time – to keep changing one's opinion
exp: 'in the teeth of' means 'in spite of strong opposition' (घोर विरोध के बावजूद). Correct meanings of the others: 'blow hot and cold' = to keep changing one's opinion; 'an acid test' = a decisive test of value or quality; 'in the nick of time' = just in time.

q: Which of the following idioms is NOT correctly matched with its meaning?
opts: True to one's salt – loyal to one's master
Keep at bay – a life full of quarrels
Paint the town red – to celebrate wildly
Give up the ghost – to die
exp: 'keep at bay' means 'to keep at a distance' (दूर रखना), not 'a life full of quarrels' (that is the meaning of 'cat and dog life'). The other pairs are correct.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'a fly in the ointment'
opts: a small flaw that spoils something
in a state of total confusion or disorder
a holiday spent doing one's usual work
to know where one's advantage lies
exp: 'a fly in the ointment' means 'a small flaw that spoils something' (Hindi: रंग में भंग, छोटी कमी). The other options are the meanings of 'know which side one's bread is buttered'; 'at sixes and sevens'; 'a busman's holiday' respectively.

q:
Match the idioms in List-I with their meanings in List-II:
List-I: (A) Beat about the bush; (B) Hang fire; (C) Burn one's fingers; (D) Pay through the nose
List-II: (1) to avoid coming to the point; (2) to be delayed; (3) to pay an excessive price; (4) to suffer loss through meddling
exp: Correct matching: 'beat about the bush' = to avoid coming to the point; 'hang fire' = to be delayed; 'burn one's fingers' = to suffer loss through meddling; 'pay through the nose' = to pay an excessive price. Hence A-1, B-2, C-4, D-3.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to agree fully'
exp: 'see eye to eye' means 'to agree fully' (Hindi: पूर्णतः सहमत होना). Others: 'a fair-weather friend' = a friend who deserts you in times of trouble; 'cut a sorry figure' = to make a poor impression; 'above board' = honest and open.

q: Which of the following idioms is NOT correctly matched with its meaning?
opts: Blow one's own trumpet – to praise oneself
Beggar description – to be impossible to describe
Die in harness – very calm and composed
A cat's paw – a person used as a tool by another
exp: 'die in harness' means 'to die while still working' (काम करते-करते मरना), not 'very calm and composed' (that is the meaning of 'as cool as a cucumber'). The other pairs are correct.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to fail to produce the intended effect'
exp: 'fall flat' means 'to fail to produce the intended effect' (Hindi: असफल होना, प्रभावहीन रहना). Others: 'a laughing stock' = an object of ridicule; 'pull one's weight' = to do one's fair share of work; 'every inch' = in every way; thoroughly (as in "every inch a gentleman").

q: Which of the following idioms is CORRECTLY matched with its meaning?
opts: Take with a pinch of salt – a practical method based on experience
Rack one's brains – to accept with some doubt
A rule of thumb – to think very hard
A white elephant – a costly possession that is useless or troublesome
exp: 'a white elephant' means 'a costly possession that is useless or troublesome' (महँगी किंतु अनुपयोगी वस्तु). Correct meanings of the others: 'a rule of thumb' = a practical method based on experience; 'rack one's brains' = to think very hard; 'take with a pinch of salt' = to accept with some doubt.

q: Which of the following idioms is CORRECTLY matched with its meaning?
opts: End in smoke – a worthless or dishonest person
Pull one's weight – to do one's fair share of work
A bad egg – a person who does not settle in one place or job
A rolling stone – to come to nothing
exp: 'pull one's weight' means 'to do one's fair share of work' (अपनी ज़िम्मेदारी निभाना). Correct meanings of the others: 'end in smoke' = to come to nothing; 'a bad egg' = a worthless or dishonest person; 'a rolling stone' = a person who does not settle in one place or job.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'a dangerous person pretending to be harmless'
opts: At the end of one's tether
exp: 'a wolf in sheep's clothing' means 'a dangerous person pretending to be harmless' (Hindi: भेड़ की खाल में भेड़िया). Others: 'a baker's dozen' = thirteen; 'build castles in the air' = to make impractical plans; to daydream; 'at the end of one's tether' = having no patience or energy left.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'human nature; one's relatives'
opts: Born with a silver spoon in one's mouth
exp: 'flesh and blood' means 'human nature; one's relatives' (Hindi: मानव स्वभाव, सगे-संबंधी). Others: 'a jack of all trades' = a person who can do many kinds of work; 'a lame excuse' = an unconvincing excuse; 'born with a silver spoon in one's mouth' = born in a rich family.

q: Which of the following idioms is NOT correctly matched with its meaning?
opts: True to one's salt – loyal to one's master
Pick holes in – to refuse to have anything more to do with
Hold one's horses – to wait and be patient
A bull in a china shop – a clumsy person in a delicate situation
exp: 'pick holes in' means 'to find fault with' (दोष निकालना), not 'to refuse to have anything more to do with' (that is the meaning of 'wash one's hands of'). The other pairs are correct.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'call it a day'
opts: to suffer in silence from grief or envy
to stop working for the day
exp: 'call it a day' means 'to stop working for the day' (Hindi: दिन का काम समाप्त करना). The other options are the meanings of 'throw cold water on'; 'stand one's ground'; 'eat one's heart out' respectively.

q: Which of the following idioms is NOT correctly matched with its meaning?
opts: Blow one's own trumpet – to praise oneself
Cast pearls before swine – to offer something valuable to those who cannot appreciate it
A thorn in the flesh – false or insincere sorrow
exp: 'a thorn in the flesh' means 'a constant source of annoyance' (लगातार परेशानी का कारण), not 'false or insincere sorrow' (that is the meaning of 'crocodile tears'). The other pairs are correct.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to avoid'
exp: 'fight shy of' means 'to avoid' (Hindi: कतराना). Others: 'a nest egg' = money saved for the future; 'take to one's heels' = to run away; 'rise like a phoenix' = to rise again after destruction.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'tongue in cheek'
exp: 'tongue in cheek' means 'not meant seriously, ironically' (Hindi: मज़ाक में, व्यंग्य में). The other options are the meanings of 'born with a silver spoon in one's mouth'; 'lose one's temper'; 'pour oil on troubled waters' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'a situation from which no progress is possible'
exp: 'a dead end' means 'a situation from which no progress is possible' (Hindi: गतिरोध). Others: 'dead letter' = a law or rule no longer in force; 'stand one's ground' = to refuse to give way; 'save one's skin' = to escape from danger or punishment.

q:
Match the idioms in List-I with their meanings in List-II:
List-I: (A) A pie in the sky; (B) Apple-pie order; (C) Tongue in cheek; (D) A green horn
List-II: (1) not meant seriously, ironically; (2) a hope or plan that is very unlikely to be realised; (3) an inexperienced person; (4) perfect order
exp: Correct matching: 'a pie in the sky' = a hope or plan that is very unlikely to be realised; 'apple-pie order' = perfect order; 'tongue in cheek' = not meant seriously, ironically; 'a green horn' = an inexperienced person. Hence A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'threat of starvation or poverty'
exp: 'a wolf at the door' means 'threat of starvation or poverty' (Hindi: भुखमरी का ख़तरा). Others: 'hold one's horses' = to wait and be patient; 'salt of the earth' = a person of great worth; 'root and branch' = thoroughly, completely.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to treat harshly without consideration'
exp: 'ride roughshod over' means 'to treat harshly without consideration' (Hindi: बेरहमी से कुचलना). Others: 'all and sundry' = everyone without distinction; 'nip in the bud' = to stop something at an early stage; 'a feather in one's cap' = an achievement to be proud of.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'something that turns out to be disappointing'
exp: 'a damp squib' means 'something that turns out to be disappointing' (Hindi: निराशाजनक परिणाम). Others: 'a dog's life' = a miserable existence; 'cut the Gordian knot' = to solve a difficult problem by bold action; 'a far-fetched idea' = an idea that is unlikely to be true.

q:
Match the idioms in List-I with their meanings in List-II:
List-I: (A) Call a spade a spade; (B) Know which side one's bread is buttered; (C) Make a mountain of a molehill; (D) All moonshine
List-II: (1) to speak plainly and frankly; (2) empty talk, nonsense; (3) to know where one's advantage lies; (4) to exaggerate a minor problem
exp: Correct matching: 'call a spade a spade' = to speak plainly and frankly; 'know which side one's bread is buttered' = to know where one's advantage lies; 'make a mountain of a molehill' = to exaggerate a minor problem; 'all moonshine' = empty talk, nonsense. Hence A-1, B-3, C-4, D-2.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'a bone of contention'
exp: 'a bone of contention' means 'a subject of dispute' (Hindi: झगड़े का विषय). The other options are the meanings of 'hit the sack'; 'flesh and blood'; 'a nest egg' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to understand the hidden meaning'
exp: 'read between the lines' means 'to understand the hidden meaning' (Hindi: छिपे अर्थ को समझना). Others: 'back out' = to withdraw from an agreement or promise; 'change hands' = to pass to another owner; 'an open secret' = something supposed to be secret but known to all.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'an axe to grind'
opts: a person who spoils the enjoyment of others
exp: 'an axe to grind' means 'a selfish motive' (Hindi: निजी स्वार्थ). The other options are the meanings of 'split hairs'; 'a wet blanket'; 'a sitting duck' respectively.

q: Which of the following idioms is NOT correctly matched with its meaning?
opts: At a stone's throw – at a very short distance
Chew the cud – to reflect or think deeply
Know the ropes – to know the details of how something is done
exp: 'all moonshine' means 'empty talk, nonsense' (बकवास), not 'thirteen' (that is the meaning of 'a baker's dozen'). The other pairs are correct.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to compensate for a wrong'
exp: 'make amends' means 'to compensate for a wrong' (Hindi: भरपाई करना). Others: 'walk on eggshells' = to be very careful not to upset someone; 'flog a dead horse' = to waste effort on a finished matter; 'at the eleventh hour' = at the last possible moment.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to meet someone more powerful than expected'
exp: 'catch a tartar' means 'to meet someone more powerful than expected' (Hindi: सेर को सवा सेर मिलना). Others: 'a dog's life' = a miserable existence; 'from the horse's mouth' = directly from the original source; 'in a jiffy' = very quickly.

q: Which of the following idioms is CORRECTLY matched with its meaning?
opts: Within an ace of – a person who can do many kinds of work
Hit the sack – very close to
Carry coal to Newcastle – to do something superfluous
A jack of all trades – to go to bed
exp: 'carry coal to Newcastle' means 'to do something superfluous' (उल्टे बाँस बरेली को). Correct meanings of the others: 'a jack of all trades' = a person who can do many kinds of work; 'hit the sack' = to go to bed; 'within an ace of' = very close to.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to find fault with'
exp: 'pick holes in' means 'to find fault with' (Hindi: दोष निकालना). Others: 'fly in the face of' = to openly defy; 'add fuel to the fire' = to make a bad situation worse; 'get the upper hand' = to gain an advantage.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'after one's own heart'
opts: to withdraw from an agreement or promise
exp: 'after one's own heart' means 'of the kind one likes' (Hindi: मनपसंद). The other options are the meanings of 'back out'; 'a song and dance'; 'fair and square' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'bag and baggage'
opts: to reveal a secret, often carelessly
exp: 'bag and baggage' means 'with all one's belongings' (Hindi: बोरिया-बिस्तर समेत). The other options are the meanings of 'spill the beans'; 'within an ace of'; 'clip someone's wings' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'under the weather'
opts: something that has no chance of success
exp: 'under the weather' means 'feeling ill' (Hindi: अस्वस्थ). The other options are the meanings of 'a song and dance'; 'set one's heart on'; 'a lost cause' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'between Scylla and Charybdis'
opts: faced with two equally dangerous choices
to try to do more than one is able to
a person used as a tool by another
to be very careful not to upset someone
exp: 'between Scylla and Charybdis' means 'faced with two equally dangerous choices' (Hindi: इधर कुआँ उधर खाई). The other options are the meanings of 'a cat's paw'; 'walk on eggshells'; 'bite off more than one can chew' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to behave in an uncontrolled way'
exp: 'run riot' means 'to behave in an uncontrolled way' (Hindi: उपद्रव मचाना). Others: 'an old flame' = a former lover; 'on the dot' = exactly on time; 'tongue in cheek' = not meant seriously, ironically.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'run amuck'
opts: an achievement to be proud of
to meet someone more powerful than expected
exp: 'run amuck' means 'to behave wildly and violently' (Hindi: उन्मत्त होकर उत्पात मचाना). The other options are the meanings of 'catch a tartar'; 'a feather in one's cap'; 'a dog's chance' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'a hard nut to crack'
opts: to do something in the easiest or cheapest way, often neglecting quality
to fail or succeed by one's own efforts
a difficult problem or person to deal with
exp: 'a hard nut to crack' means 'a difficult problem or person to deal with' (Hindi: कठिन समस्या या व्यक्ति). The other options are the meanings of 'sink or swim'; 'bag and baggage'; 'cut corners' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to have both good and bad effects'
exp: 'cut both ways' means 'to have both good and bad effects' (Hindi: दोधारी, लाभ-हानि दोनों). Others: 'a dead end' = a situation from which no progress is possible; 'walk of life' = occupation or profession; 'a red letter day' = a memorable or important day.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'hold one's horses'
exp: 'hold one's horses' means 'to wait and be patient' (Hindi: धैर्य रखना, रुकना). The other options are the meanings of 'keep body and soul together'; 'hole and corner'; 'out of the wood' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to die while still working'
exp: 'die in harness' means 'to die while still working' (Hindi: काम करते-करते मरना). Others: 'a Himalayan blunder' = a very big mistake; 'go the whole hog' = to do something thoroughly; 'throw down the gauntlet' = to issue a challenge.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'something that attracts attention for a short time'
exp: 'a nine days' wonder' means 'something that attracts attention for a short time' (Hindi: क्षणिक आकर्षण की वस्तु). Others: 'safe and sound' = unharmed; 'break the ice' = to start a conversation in a formal or awkward situation; 'die hard' = to change or disappear very slowly.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'a red letter day'
opts: to have no influence or effect
a person who keeps his promises
exp: 'a red letter day' means 'a memorable or important day' (Hindi: यादगार/महत्वपूर्ण दिन). The other options are the meanings of 'a man of his word'; 'get wind of'; 'cut no ice' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'leave in the lurch'
opts: to make the best use of an opportunity
the ability to speak fluently and persuasively
to be satisfied with past success and stop trying
exp: 'leave in the lurch' means 'to desert someone in difficulty' (Hindi: मुसीबत में साथ छोड़ना). The other options are the meanings of 'make hay while the sun shines'; 'a gift of the gab'; 'rest on one's laurels' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'a lame excuse'
opts: to behave in an uncontrolled way
the final problem that makes a situation unbearable
exp: 'a lame excuse' means 'an unconvincing excuse' (Hindi: लचर बहाना). The other options are the meanings of 'run riot'; 'the last straw'; 'tooth and nail' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'a square meal'
opts: to make something orderly or efficient
exp: 'a square meal' means 'a full and satisfying meal' (Hindi: भरपेट भोजन). The other options are the meanings of 'knock into shape'; 'rank and file'; 'let the cat out of the bag' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'a person who neither uses a thing himself nor lets others use it'
exp: 'dog in the manger' means 'a person who neither uses a thing himself nor lets others use it' (Hindi: न खाए न खाने दे). Others: 'a skeleton in the cupboard' = a shameful secret; 'a fool's errand' = a task that has no hope of success; 'an ugly duckling' = a plain child who grows into a beautiful adult.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'cast pearls before swine'
opts: to offer something valuable to those who cannot appreciate it
to be satisfied with past success and stop trying
exp: 'cast pearls before swine' means 'to offer something valuable to those who cannot appreciate it' (Hindi: भैंस के आगे बीन बजाना). The other options are the meanings of 'in a nutshell'; 'cheek by jowl'; 'rest on one's laurels' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'fish in troubled waters'
opts: to take an action that cannot be reversed
to remain neutral; to be undecided
to shift responsibility to someone else
to take advantage of a confused situation
exp: 'fish in troubled waters' means 'to take advantage of a confused situation' (Hindi: बहती गंगा में हाथ धोना (अशांति का लाभ उठाना)). The other options are the meanings of 'sit on the fence'; 'burn one's boats'; 'pass the buck' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to die (informal)'
exp: 'kick the bucket' means 'to die (informal)' (Hindi: मर जाना). Others: 'as bold as brass' = very confident and shameless; 'keep up appearances' = to maintain an outward show; 'fight shy of' = to avoid.

q:
Match the idioms in List-I with their meanings in List-II:
List-I: (A) Miss the boat; (B) Cold comfort; (C) Over head and ears; (D) Keep one's fingers crossed
List-II: (1) to hope for the best; (2) little or no consolation; (3) deeply, completely (in debt or love); (4) to lose an opportunity
exp: Correct matching: 'miss the boat' = to lose an opportunity; 'cold comfort' = little or no consolation; 'over head and ears' = deeply, completely (in debt or love); 'keep one's fingers crossed' = to hope for the best. Hence A-4, B-2, C-3, D-1.

q:
Match the idioms in List-I with their meanings in List-II:
List-I: (A) Set the Thames on fire; (B) Show a clean pair of heels; (C) An ivory tower; (D) Pay lip service
List-II: (1) to support in words but not in deeds; (2) to do something remarkable; (3) a state of isolation from the practical realities of life; (4) to run away quickly and escape
exp: Correct matching: 'set the Thames on fire' = to do something remarkable; 'show a clean pair of heels' = to run away quickly and escape; 'an ivory tower' = a state of isolation from the practical realities of life; 'pay lip service' = to support in words but not in deeds. Hence A-2, B-4, C-3, D-1.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'listening eagerly'
exp: 'all ears' means 'listening eagerly' (Hindi: पूरे ध्यान से सुनना). Others: 'once in a blue moon' = very rarely; 'a narrow escape' = escape from danger with very little margin; 'red tape' = excessive bureaucratic formality.

q: Which of the following idioms is NOT correctly matched with its meaning?
opts: A lame excuse – an unconvincing excuse
Have a finger in every pie – to be involved in many activities
In high spirits – to experience financial hardship
Fish in troubled waters – to take advantage of a confused situation
exp: 'in high spirits' means 'very cheerful' (अत्यंत प्रसन्न), not 'to experience financial hardship' (that is the meaning of 'feel the pinch'). The other pairs are correct.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to run away'
exp: 'take to one's heels' means 'to run away' (Hindi: भाग खड़ा होना). Others: 'rack one's brains' = to think very hard; 'pull strings' = to use one's influence secretly; 'out of sorts' = slightly unwell or upset.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'superior to'
exp: 'a cut above' means 'superior to' (Hindi: से श्रेष्ठ). Others: 'a fish out of water' = a person in an unfamiliar and uncomfortable situation; 'at large' = free and not captured; 'in cold blood' = deliberately and cruelly.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to share the cost equally'
opts: At the drop of a hat
exp: 'go Dutch' means 'to share the cost equally' (Hindi: अपना-अपना ख़र्च उठाना). Others: 'at the drop of a hat' = immediately, without hesitation; 'take to task' = to rebuke; 'add fuel to the fire' = to make a bad situation worse.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'eat one's words'
opts: to take back what one has said
to do something never done before
exp: 'eat one's words' means 'to take back what one has said' (Hindi: अपनी बात वापस लेना). The other options are the meanings of 'break new ground'; 'with a high hand'; 'at large' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to lose an opportunity'
exp: 'miss the boat' means 'to lose an opportunity' (Hindi: अवसर गँवाना). Others: 'lay one's hands on' = to obtain or get hold of; 'once in a blue moon' = very rarely; 'rise to the occasion' = to deal successfully with a difficult situation.

q: Which of the following idioms is NOT correctly matched with its meaning?
opts: At a premium – to keep quiet
True to one's salt – loyal to one's master
Knock into shape – to make something orderly or efficient
By the skin of one's teeth – only just; narrowly
exp: 'at a premium' means 'in great demand; scarce' (बहुत माँग में), not 'to keep quiet' (that is the meaning of 'hold one's tongue'). The other pairs are correct.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to desert someone in difficulty'
exp: 'leave in the lurch' means 'to desert someone in difficulty' (Hindi: मुसीबत में साथ छोड़ना). Others: 'make amends' = to compensate for a wrong; 'beggar description' = to be impossible to describe; 'all moonshine' = empty talk, nonsense.

q: Which of the following idioms is CORRECTLY matched with its meaning?
opts: Rack one's brains – to use one's influence secretly
Rise like a phoenix – to think very hard
A penny for your thoughts – a request to know what someone is thinking
Pull strings – to rise again after destruction
exp: 'a penny for your thoughts' means 'a request to know what someone is thinking' (तुम क्या सोच रहे हो). Correct meanings of the others: 'pull strings' = to use one's influence secretly; 'rise like a phoenix' = to rise again after destruction; 'rack one's brains' = to think very hard.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to remain calm in a crisis'
exp: 'keep one's head' means 'to remain calm in a crisis' (Hindi: संकट में शांत रहना). Others: 'in the good books' = in favour; 'win hands down' = to win easily; 'a cold war' = a state of hostility without actual fighting.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'give the cold shoulder'
opts: to treat someone with deliberate coldness
exp: 'give the cold shoulder' means 'to treat someone with deliberate coldness' (Hindi: उपेक्षा करना, रूखा व्यवहार). The other options are the meanings of 'hit below the belt'; 'paint the town red'; 'cat and dog life' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'take into account'
exp: 'take into account' means 'to consider' (Hindi: ध्यान में रखना). The other options are the meanings of 'win hands down'; 'stand one's ground'; 'with a high hand' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to do something never done before'
exp: 'break new ground' means 'to do something never done before' (Hindi: नई शुरुआत करना, नया काम करना). Others: 'cut both ways' = to have both good and bad effects; 'a song and dance' = a fuss; 'get wind of' = to hear about something secretly.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'thirteen'
exp: 'a baker's dozen' means 'thirteen' (Hindi: तेरह). Others: 'an Achilles' heel' = a weak point; 'weal and woe' = prosperity and adversity; 'run amuck' = to behave wildly and violently.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to wait and be patient'
opts: Put a spoke in one's wheel
exp: 'hold one's horses' means 'to wait and be patient' (Hindi: धैर्य रखना, रुकना). Others: 'put a spoke in one's wheel' = to obstruct someone's plans; 'rain cats and dogs' = to rain very heavily; 'wash one's hands of' = to refuse to have anything more to do with.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'bring to light'
opts: to punish or call to account
exp: 'bring to light' means 'to reveal' (Hindi: प्रकाश में लाना). The other options are the meanings of 'bring to book'; 'by word of mouth'; 'carry the day' respectively.

q: Which of the following idioms is CORRECTLY matched with its meaning?
opts: On the horns of a dilemma – to spoil a plan
Upset the apple cart – the beginning and the end
Alpha and omega – in a situation requiring a choice between two unpleasant alternatives
An eye-opener – something that reveals a surprising truth
exp: 'an eye-opener' means 'something that reveals a surprising truth' (आँखें खोलने वाली बात). Correct meanings of the others: 'alpha and omega' = the beginning and the end; 'on the horns of a dilemma' = in a situation requiring a choice between two unpleasant alternatives; 'upset the apple cart' = to spoil a plan.

q: Which of the following idioms is CORRECTLY matched with its meaning?
opts: Hit the nail on the head – to say exactly the right thing
Hand in glove – already decided and unlikely to change
Cut and dried – to suspect something wrong
Smell a rat – very intimate, working closely together (often in wrongdoing)
exp: 'hit the nail on the head' means 'to say exactly the right thing' (बिल्कुल सही बात कहना). Correct meanings of the others: 'cut and dried' = already decided and unlikely to change; 'smell a rat' = to suspect something wrong; 'hand in glove' = very intimate, working closely together (often in wrongdoing).

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'with open arms'
opts: to start a conversation in a formal or awkward situation
exp: 'with open arms' means 'warmly, with great welcome' (Hindi: गर्मजोशी से). The other options are the meanings of 'break the ice'; 'take French leave'; 'blue blood' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'dead letter'
opts: to have both good and bad effects
a law or rule no longer in force
exp: 'dead letter' means 'a law or rule no longer in force' (Hindi: निष्प्रभावी नियम). The other options are the meanings of 'cut both ways'; 'in cold blood'; 'off and on' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'add fuel to the fire'
opts: to try to win popular approval
to make a bad situation worse
exp: 'add fuel to the fire' means 'to make a bad situation worse' (Hindi: आग में घी डालना). The other options are the meanings of 'play to the gallery'; 'a square meal'; 'in the teeth of' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to flatter servilely'
opts: Put the cart before the horse
exp: 'lick one's boots' means 'to flatter servilely' (Hindi: चापलूसी करना). Others: 'skate on thin ice' = to be in a risky situation; 'put the cart before the horse' = to do things in the wrong order; 'by fits and starts' = irregularly; not continuously.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'warmly, with great welcome'
exp: 'with open arms' means 'warmly, with great welcome' (Hindi: गर्मजोशी से). Others: 'blue blood' = of noble birth; 'make up one's mind' = to decide; 'walk of life' = occupation or profession.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to praise oneself'
exp: 'blow one's own trumpet' means 'to praise oneself' (Hindi: अपने मुँह मियाँ मिट्ठू बनना). Others: 'all thumbs' = very clumsy with one's hands; 'play second fiddle' = to take a subordinate role; 'at daggers drawn' = bitterly hostile to each other.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'put one's foot in it'
exp: 'put one's foot in it' means 'to say something tactless' (Hindi: बेतुकी बात कह देना). The other options are the meanings of 'lose one's head'; 'give in'; 'give a piece of one's mind' respectively.

q: Which of the following idioms is CORRECTLY matched with its meaning?
opts: A black sheep – to calm a quarrel
Take the bull by the horns – to face a difficulty boldly
Pour oil on troubled waters – to maintain an outward show
Keep up appearances – a person who brings disgrace to the family or group
exp: 'take the bull by the horns' means 'to face a difficulty boldly' (साहस से कठिनाई का सामना करना). Correct meanings of the others: 'keep up appearances' = to maintain an outward show; 'a black sheep' = a person who brings disgrace to the family or group; 'pour oil on troubled waters' = to calm a quarrel.

q: Which of the following idioms is NOT correctly matched with its meaning?
opts: Cast a slur – the ability to speak fluently and persuasively
Die in harness – to die while still working
Live in a fool's paradise – to have a false sense of happiness
As dead as a dodo – completely extinct or out of date
exp: 'cast a slur' means 'to bring disgrace to' (कलंक लगाना), not 'the ability to speak fluently and persuasively' (that is the meaning of 'a gift of the gab'). The other pairs are correct.

q:
Match the idioms in List-I with their meanings in List-II:
List-I: (A) Out of the wood; (B) Bear in mind; (C) A bone to pick; (D) At random
List-II: (1) without any plan or purpose; (2) to remember; (3) a matter to complain or argue about; (4) out of danger or difficulty
exp: Correct matching: 'out of the wood' = out of danger or difficulty; 'bear in mind' = to remember; 'a bone to pick' = a matter to complain or argue about; 'at random' = without any plan or purpose. Hence A-4, B-2, C-3, D-1.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'in trouble'
exp: 'in hot water' means 'in trouble' (Hindi: मुसीबत में). Others: 'get cold feet' = to become nervous and lose courage; 'by word of mouth' = orally, by spoken words; 'give in' = to surrender; to stop resisting.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'put up with'
exp: 'put up with' means 'to tolerate' (Hindi: सहन करना). The other options are the meanings of 'safe and sound'; 'up in arms'; 'in the air' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'go against the grain'
opts: to make a painful situation worse
to be contrary to one's nature
a person who brings disgrace to the family or group
exp: 'go against the grain' means 'to be contrary to one's nature' (Hindi: स्वभाव के विरुद्ध होना). The other options are the meanings of 'a black sheep'; 'rub salt into the wound'; 'hit the sack' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'read between the lines'
opts: a person in an unfamiliar and uncomfortable situation
a law or rule no longer in force

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'ordinary members of an organisation'
exp: 'rank and file' means 'ordinary members of an organisation' (Hindi: साधारण सदस्य). Others: 'call the shots' = to be in charge and make decisions; 'fly off the handle' = to lose one's temper suddenly; 'neck and neck' = level in a race or competition.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'take French leave'
exp: 'take French leave' means 'to leave without permission' (Hindi: बिना अनुमति चले जाना). The other options are the meanings of 'up to the mark'; 'win hands down'; 'set one's heart on' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'a person in an unfamiliar and uncomfortable situation'
exp: 'a fish out of water' means 'a person in an unfamiliar and uncomfortable situation' (Hindi: असहज स्थिति में व्यक्ति). Others: 'off and on' = occasionally; 'put up with' = to tolerate; 'bring to book' = to punish or call to account.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'come off with flying colours'
opts: to do things in the wrong order
exp: 'come off with flying colours' means 'to succeed brilliantly' (Hindi: शानदार सफलता पाना). The other options are the meanings of 'dance to someone's tune'; 'put the cart before the horse'; 'bag and baggage' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'the first speech of a person in parliament or public'
exp: 'a maiden speech' means 'the first speech of a person in parliament or public' (Hindi: पहला भाषण). Others: 'as busy as a bee' = very busy; 'a sitting duck' = an easy target; 'lend an ear' = to listen attentively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'under one's thumb'
opts: a costly possession that is useless or troublesome
to take an action that cannot be reversed
exp: 'under one's thumb' means 'completely under one's control' (Hindi: किसी के वश में). The other options are the meanings of 'burn one's boats'; 'a snake in the grass'; 'a white elephant' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'come to terms with'
opts: to have no influence or effect
exp: 'come to terms with' means 'to accept a difficult situation' (Hindi: स्थिति को स्वीकार करना). The other options are the meanings of 'call off'; 'few and far between'; 'cut no ice' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'a cause of quarrel'
exp: 'an apple of discord' means 'a cause of quarrel' (Hindi: झगड़े की जड़). Others: 'a thorn in the flesh' = a constant source of annoyance; 'haul over the coals' = to scold severely; 'call a spade a spade' = to speak plainly and frankly.

q: Which of the following idioms is NOT correctly matched with its meaning?

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'bury the hatchet'
opts: at a distance, avoiding close contact
to make peace and end a quarrel
exp: 'bury the hatchet' means 'to make peace and end a quarrel' (Hindi: पुरानी दुश्मनी भुलाकर मेल करना). The other options are the meanings of 'as fit as a fiddle'; 'at arm's length'; 'leave in the lurch' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to obey someone without question'
exp: 'dance to someone's tune' means 'to obey someone without question' (Hindi: किसी के इशारों पर नाचना). Others: 'turn over a new leaf' = to change one's behaviour for the better; 'sit on the fence' = to remain neutral; to be undecided; 'beside the mark' = irrelevant.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'dog in the manger'

to stop something at an early stage
exp: 'dog in the manger' means 'a person who neither uses a thing himself nor lets others use it' (Hindi: न खाए न खाने दे). The other options are the meanings of 'crocodile tears'; 'a dog's chance'; 'nip in the bud' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'turn over a new leaf'
opts: to change one's behaviour for the better
exp: 'turn over a new leaf' means 'to change one's behaviour for the better' (Hindi: आचरण सुधारना, नई शुरुआत करना). The other options are the meanings of 'come off with flying colours'; 'head over heels'; 'keep up appearances' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to take a subordinate role'
exp: 'play second fiddle' means 'to take a subordinate role' (Hindi: अधीनस्थ भूमिका निभाना). Others: 'haul over the coals' = to scold severely; 'all and sundry' = everyone without distinction; 'in a jiffy' = very quickly.

q: Which of the following idioms is CORRECTLY matched with its meaning?
opts: Cast a slur – very useful service or help

exp: 'in a jiffy' means 'very quickly' (पल भर में). Correct meanings of the others: 'cast a slur' = to bring disgrace to; 'yeoman's service' = very useful service or help; 'an armchair critic' = one who criticises without practical experience.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to deceive'
exp: 'throw dust in one's eyes' means 'to deceive' (Hindi: आँखों में धूल झोंकना). Others: 'true to one's salt' = loyal to one's master; 'neck and neck' = level in a race or competition; 'in the pink' = in very good health and spirits.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'go through fire and water'
opts: to face all kinds of risks and dangers
to withdraw from an agreement or promise
to draw a conclusion from facts
exp: 'go through fire and water' means 'to face all kinds of risks and dangers' (Hindi: हर संकट का सामना करना). The other options are the meanings of 'put two and two together'; 'down to earth'; 'back out' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'the beginning and the end'
exp: 'alpha and omega' means 'the beginning and the end' (Hindi: आदि और अंत). Others: 'flesh and blood' = human nature; one's relatives; 'a cock and bull story' = an absurd, unbelievable story; 'a queer fish' = a strange person.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'a damp squib'
opts: something that turns out to be disappointing
to be satisfied with past success and stop trying

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'by fits and starts'
opts: to take advantage of a confused situation
exp: 'by fits and starts' means 'irregularly; not continuously' (Hindi: रुक-रुककर). The other options are the meanings of 'carry coal to Newcastle'; 'fish in troubled waters'; 'a close shave' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'break the ice'
opts: to start a conversation in a formal or awkward situation
exp: 'break the ice' means 'to start a conversation in a formal or awkward situation' (Hindi: झिझक तोड़ना, बातचीत शुरू करना). The other options are the meanings of 'do away with'; 'a shot in the dark'; 'at large' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to face all kinds of risks and dangers'
exp: 'go through fire and water' means 'to face all kinds of risks and dangers' (Hindi: हर संकट का सामना करना). Others: 'fall to one's lot' = to become one's fate or duty; 'see eye to eye' = to agree fully; 'in the air' = uncertain; being rumoured.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'a person of no substance or means'
exp: 'a man of straw' means 'a person of no substance or means' (Hindi: कमज़ोर या साधनहीन व्यक्ति). Others: 'a bed of roses' = an easy and comfortable situation; 'feel the pinch' = to experience financial hardship; 'draw in one's horns' = to become more cautious; to reduce spending.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'strict and fixed (rule)'
exp: 'hard and fast' means 'strict and fixed (rule)' (Hindi: कठोर और निश्चित). Others: 'call it a day' = to stop working for the day; 'eat one's heart out' = to suffer in silence from grief or envy; 'the talk of the town' = a person or thing everyone is talking about.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'a former lover'
exp: 'an old flame' means 'a former lover' (Hindi: पुराना प्रेमी/प्रेमिका). Others: 'keep up appearances' = to maintain an outward show; 'run riot' = to behave in an uncontrolled way; 'a pie in the sky' = a hope or plan that is very unlikely to be realised.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to refuse to give way'
exp: 'stand one's ground' means 'to refuse to give way' (Hindi: डटे रहना). Others: 'call it a day' = to stop working for the day; 'lose one's head' = to become confused or excited; 'cut both ways' = to have both good and bad effects.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'a green horn'
opts: to be contrary to one's nature
exp: 'a green horn' means 'an inexperienced person' (Hindi: अनाड़ी, नौसिखिया). The other options are the meanings of 'a bolt from the blue'; 'upset the apple cart'; 'go against the grain' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to take advantage of a confused situation'
exp: 'fish in troubled waters' means 'to take advantage of a confused situation' (Hindi: बहती गंगा में हाथ धोना (अशांति का लाभ उठाना)). Others: 'hand in glove' = very intimate, working closely together (often in wrongdoing); 'on the dot' = exactly on time; 'a penny for your thoughts' = a request to know what someone is thinking.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'thoroughly; completely'

exp: 'to the backbone' means 'thoroughly; completely' (Hindi: पूर्णतः, पक्का). Others: 'a turncoat' = a person who changes sides or principles; 'know which side one's bread is buttered' = to know where one's advantage lies; 'dog in the manger' = a person who neither uses a thing himself nor lets others use it.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'take with a pinch of salt'
opts: to behave in an uncontrolled way
exp: 'take with a pinch of salt' means 'to accept with some doubt' (Hindi: संदेह के साथ स्वीकार करना). The other options are the meanings of 'tooth and nail'; 'bag and baggage'; 'run riot' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'false or insincere sorrow'
exp: 'crocodile tears' means 'false or insincere sorrow' (Hindi: घड़ियाली आँसू). Others: 'a fool's errand' = a task that has no hope of success; 'lion's share' = the largest part; 'a baker's dozen' = thirteen.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'a shot in the dark'
exp: 'a shot in the dark' means 'a wild guess' (Hindi: अटकलबाज़ी, अंधेरे में तीर). The other options are the meanings of 'win hands down'; 'black and blue'; 'a man of parts' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'go back on one's word'
opts: a law or rule no longer in force
exp: 'go back on one's word' means 'to break a promise' (Hindi: वचन से मुकर जाना). The other options are the meanings of 'with open arms'; 'hold water'; 'dead letter' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'bear the brunt'
opts: to bear the main burden or impact
to face criticism or danger from many sides
exp: 'bear the brunt' means 'to bear the main burden or impact' (Hindi: मुख्य भार सहना). The other options are the meanings of 'of no avail'; 'run the gauntlet'; 'let bygones be bygones' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to ask for something impossible'
exp: 'cry for the moon' means 'to ask for something impossible' (Hindi: असंभव वस्तु की माँग करना). Others: 'behind the scenes' = secretly, in private; 'worth one's salt' = competent and deserving one's pay; 'in the pink' = in very good health and spirits.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'wash dirty linen in public'
opts: to discuss private quarrels in public
a large payment given to someone leaving a job
exp: 'wash dirty linen in public' means 'to discuss private quarrels in public' (Hindi: घर की बात बाहर करना). The other options are the meanings of 'as cool as a cucumber'; 'a golden handshake'; 'donkey's years' respectively.

q: Which of the following idioms is NOT correctly matched with its meaning?
opts: Grease the palm – to know the details of how something is done
A feather in one's cap – an achievement to be proud of
At sixes and sevens – in a state of total confusion or disorder
An armchair critic – one who criticises without practical experience
exp: 'grease the palm' means 'to bribe' (रिश्वत देना), not 'to know the details of how something is done' (that is the meaning of 'know the ropes'). The other pairs are correct.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'a task that has no hope of success'
exp: 'a fool's errand' means 'a task that has no hope of success' (Hindi: व्यर्थ का काम). Others: 'spick and span' = neat and clean; 'blow one's own trumpet' = to praise oneself; 'know the ropes' = to know the details of how something is done.

q: Which of the following idioms is NOT correctly matched with its meaning?

A nest egg – money saved for the future
A wild goose chase – a costly possession that is useless or troublesome
Clip someone's wings – to restrict someone's freedom
exp: 'a wild goose chase' means 'a foolish and hopeless search or pursuit' (व्यर्थ की खोज), not 'a costly possession that is useless or troublesome' (that is the meaning of 'a white elephant'). The other pairs are correct.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'immediately, without hesitation'
opts: At the drop of a hat
exp: 'at the drop of a hat' means 'immediately, without hesitation' (Hindi: तुरंत, बिना झिझक). Others: 'lay one's hands on' = to obtain or get hold of; 'pick holes in' = to find fault with; 'through thick and thin' = under all circumstances.

q:
Match the idioms in List-I with their meanings in List-II:

exp: Correct matching: 'dog in the manger' = a person who neither uses a thing himself nor lets others use it; 'put on airs' = to behave arrogantly; 'a Himalayan blunder' = a very big mistake; 'a pretty kettle of fish' = an awkward or difficult situation. Hence A-4, B-2, C-3, D-1.

exp: 'by word of mouth' means 'orally, by spoken words' (Hindi: मौखिक रूप से). The other options are the meanings of 'call off'; 'under the weather'; 'see red' respectively.

at a distance, avoiding close contact

q: Which of the following idioms is CORRECTLY matched with its meaning?
opts: Keep the wolf from the door – escape from danger with very little margin
Lay down one's arms – to surrender
Play to the gallery – to avoid starvation
A narrow escape – to try to win popular approval
exp: 'lay down one's arms' means 'to surrender' (हथियार डालना). Correct meanings of the others: 'a narrow escape' = escape from danger with very little margin; 'play to the gallery' = to try to win popular approval; 'keep the wolf from the door' = to avoid starvation.

exp: 'bad blood' means 'ill feeling or enmity' (Hindi: वैमनस्य, दुश्मनी). The other options are the meanings of 'on the house'; 'fair and square'; 'call off' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'a leap in the dark'
opts: to take advantage of a confused situation
a foolish and hopeless search or pursuit
an action whose result cannot be foreseen
exp: 'a leap in the dark' means 'an action whose result cannot be foreseen' (Hindi: अंधेरे में छलाँग, जोखिम भरा क़दम). The other options are the meanings of 'a wild goose chase'; 'pour oil on troubled waters'; 'fish in troubled waters' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to be contrary to one's nature'

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'mutual concession or compromise'
exp: 'give and take' means 'mutual concession or compromise' (Hindi: लेन-देन, समझौता). Others: 'set one's heart on' = to desire greatly; 'cut to the quick' = to hurt deeply; 'put two and two together' = to draw a conclusion from facts.

q:
Match the idioms in List-I with their meanings in List-II:
List-I: (A) At the eleventh hour; (B) Mince matters; (C) At sixes and sevens; (D) Between Scylla and Charybdis
List-II: (1) at the last possible moment; (2) faced with two equally dangerous choices; (3) to speak evasively to avoid offending; (4) in a state of total confusion or disorder
exp: Correct matching: 'at the eleventh hour' = at the last possible moment; 'mince matters' = to speak evasively to avoid offending; 'at sixes and sevens' = in a state of total confusion or disorder; 'between Scylla and Charybdis' = faced with two equally dangerous choices. Hence A-1, B-3, C-4, D-2.

q: Which of the following idioms is CORRECTLY matched with its meaning?
opts: At a stone's throw – everyone without distinction
All and sundry – in very good health
As fit as a fiddle – at a very short distance
Mince matters – to speak evasively to avoid offending
exp: 'mince matters' means 'to speak evasively to avoid offending' (बात को घुमाकर नरम करना). Correct meanings of the others: 'as fit as a fiddle' = in very good health; 'at a stone's throw' = at a very short distance; 'all and sundry' = everyone without distinction.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'a maiden speech'
opts: a hope or plan that is very unlikely to be realised
to be dismissed from a job
the first speech of a person in parliament or public
exp: 'a maiden speech' means 'the first speech of a person in parliament or public' (Hindi: पहला भाषण). The other options are the meanings of 'a pie in the sky'; 'get the sack'; 'lose one's temper' respectively.

q:
Match the idioms in List-I with their meanings in List-II:
List-I: (A) Get the sack; (B) By fits and starts; (C) Fish in troubled waters; (D) Pay lip service
List-II: (1) to take advantage of a confused situation; (2) irregularly; not continuously; (3) to support in words but not in deeds; (4) to be dismissed from a job
exp: Correct matching: 'get the sack' = to be dismissed from a job; 'by fits and starts' = irregularly; not continuously; 'fish in troubled waters' = to take advantage of a confused situation; 'pay lip service' = to support in words but not in deeds. Hence A-4, B-2, C-1, D-3.

to give credit even to a bad person
a sudden success that is not repeated
exp: 'by the skin of one's teeth' means 'only just; narrowly' (Hindi: बाल-बाल). The other options are the meanings of 'a flash in the pan'; 'play to the gallery'; 'give the devil his due' respectively.

q: Which of the following idioms is NOT correctly matched with its meaning?
opts: Turn the tables – to reverse a situation to one's advantage

q: Which of the following idioms is CORRECTLY matched with its meaning?

All thumbs – a difficult task or situation

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to know where one's advantage lies'

to bear the main burden or impact

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'ill feeling or enmity'

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'eat crow'

a state of isolation from the practical realities of life

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'a cry in the wilderness'
opts: to become more cautious; to reduce spending

exp: 'a laughing stock' means 'an object of ridicule' (Hindi: हँसी का पात्र). Others: 'below the belt' = unfair, against the rules; 'make a clean breast of' = to confess fully; 'in the teeth of' = in spite of strong opposition.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'at random'
exp: 'at random' means 'without any plan or purpose' (Hindi: बेतरतीब, बिना सोचे). The other options are the meanings of 'blow hot and cold'; 'red tape'; 'keep body and soul together' respectively.

q:
Match the idioms in List-I with their meanings in List-II:
List-I: (A) From the horse's mouth; (B) An Achilles' heel; (C) Call a spade a spade; (D) Make hay while the sun shines
List-II: (1) a weak point; (2) directly from the original source; (3) to speak plainly and frankly; (4) to make the best use of an opportunity
exp: Correct matching: 'from the horse's mouth' = directly from the original source; 'an Achilles' heel' = a weak point; 'call a spade a spade' = to speak plainly and frankly; 'make hay while the sun shines' = to make the best use of an opportunity. Hence A-2, B-1, C-3, D-4.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'a good Samaritan'
opts: a person who helps others in need unselfishly
to offer something valuable to those who cannot appreciate it
an idea that is unlikely to be true
exp: 'a good Samaritan' means 'a person who helps others in need unselfishly' (Hindi: परोपकारी व्यक्ति). The other options are the meanings of 'cast pearls before swine'; 'at daggers drawn'; 'a far-fetched idea' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'in a tight corner'
opts: to achieve two aims with a single action
in a difficult situation with little room to escape
to find fault with a gift
a little-known person who unexpectedly wins or succeeds
exp: 'in a tight corner' means 'in a difficult situation with little room to escape' (Hindi: कठिन स्थिति में). The other options are the meanings of 'a dark horse'; 'look a gift horse in the mouth'; 'kill two birds with one stone' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'fair and square'
exp: 'fair and square' means 'honestly and fairly' (Hindi: ईमानदारी से). The other options are the meanings of 'give in'; 'throw cold water on'; 'lose one's head' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'in the nick of time'
opts: level in a race or competition
exp: 'in the nick of time' means 'just in time' (Hindi: ठीक समय पर). The other options are the meanings of 'at random'; 'a laughing stock'; 'neck and neck' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'a race or contest in which two finish exactly level'
exp: 'a dead heat' means 'a race or contest in which two finish exactly level' (Hindi: बराबरी का मुक़ाबला). Others: 'see eye to eye' = to agree fully; 'put two and two together' = to draw a conclusion from facts; 'set one's heart on' = to desire greatly.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to refuse to have anything more to do with'
exp: 'wash one's hands of' means 'to refuse to have anything more to do with' (Hindi: पल्ला झाड़ लेना). Others: 'rank and file' = ordinary members of an organisation; 'hold one's horses' = to wait and be patient; 'an iron hand' = strict and harsh control.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'blow one's own trumpet'
opts: to regret something that cannot be undone
exp: 'blow one's own trumpet' means 'to praise oneself' (Hindi: अपने मुँह मियाँ मिट्ठू बनना). The other options are the meanings of 'a stone's throw'; 'leave no stone unturned'; 'cry over spilt milk' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to be in charge and make decisions'
opts: Put a spoke in one's wheel
exp: 'call the shots' means 'to be in charge and make decisions' (Hindi: निर्णय लेने का अधिकार रखना). Others: 'put a spoke in one's wheel' = to obstruct someone's plans; 'a wolf at the door' = threat of starvation or poverty; 'a tall order' = a very difficult demand.

q: Which of the following idioms is CORRECTLY matched with its meaning?
opts: Ups and downs – good and bad times
Feel the pinch – to be in a risky situation
Beside the mark – to experience financial hardship
exp: 'ups and downs' means 'good and bad times' (उतार-चढ़ाव). Correct meanings of the others: 'feel the pinch' = to experience financial hardship; 'skate on thin ice' = to be in a risky situation; 'beside the mark' = irrelevant.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'cool one's heels'
exp: 'cool one's heels' means 'to be kept waiting' (Hindi: प्रतीक्षा करते रहना). The other options are the meanings of 'dance to someone's tune'; 'make one's blood boil'; 'beside the mark' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'wash one's hands of'
opts: to refuse to have anything more to do with
exp: 'wash one's hands of' means 'to refuse to have anything more to do with' (Hindi: पल्ला झाड़ लेना). The other options are the meanings of 'cry for the moon'; 'under a cloud'; 'put a spoke in one's wheel' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'cry for the moon'
opts: to make progress; to become more popular
exp: 'cry for the moon' means 'to ask for something impossible' (Hindi: असंभव वस्तु की माँग करना). The other options are the meanings of 'burn one's fingers'; 'on the cards'; 'gain ground' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'crocodile tears'
opts: something that turns out to be disappointing
exp: 'crocodile tears' means 'false or insincere sorrow' (Hindi: घड़ियाली आँसू). The other options are the meanings of 'a damp squib'; 'leave in the lurch'; 'yeoman's service' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'lose one's head'
exp: 'lose one's head' means 'to become confused or excited' (Hindi: होश खो बैठना). The other options are the meanings of 'call off'; 'lose heart'; 'go back on one's word' respectively.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'to use one's influence secretly'
exp: 'pull strings' means 'to use one's influence secretly' (Hindi: सिफ़ारिश लगाना, प्रभाव का प्रयोग). Others: 'a wild goose chase' = a foolish and hopeless search or pursuit; 'sit on the fence' = to remain neutral; to be undecided; 'a hard nut to crack' = a difficult problem or person to deal with.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'without preparation'
exp: 'off the cuff' means 'without preparation' (Hindi: बिना तैयारी के). Others: 'from the horse's mouth' = directly from the original source; 'by leaps and bounds' = very rapidly; 'a feather in one's cap' = an achievement to be proud of.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'in serious difficulty, likely to fail'
exp: 'on the rocks' means 'in serious difficulty, likely to fail' (Hindi: संकट में, टूटने के कगार पर). Others: 'fly off the handle' = to lose one's temper suddenly; 'a rolling stone' = a person who does not settle in one place or job; 'rise to the occasion' = to deal successfully with a difficult situation.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'down to earth'
opts: a friend who deserts you in times of trouble
to start a conversation in a formal or awkward situation
exp: 'down to earth' means 'practical and realistic' (Hindi: व्यावहारिक). The other options are the meanings of 'break the ice'; 'call off'; 'a fair-weather friend' respectively.

opts: Pick holes in – to find fault with
Cold comfort – little or no consolation
A drop in the ocean – a decisive test of value or quality
exp: 'a drop in the ocean' means 'a very small amount compared with what is needed' (ऊँट के मुँह में जीरा), not 'a decisive test of value or quality' (that is the meaning of 'an acid test'). The other pairs are correct.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'at the drop of a hat'

a person very like his father or mother
exp: 'at the drop of a hat' means 'immediately, without hesitation' (Hindi: तुरंत, बिना झिझक). The other options are the meanings of 'pull one's leg'; 'a chip off the old block'; 'rank and file' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'all at sea'
exp: 'all at sea' means 'completely confused' (Hindi: पूरी तरह उलझन में). The other options are the meanings of 'a shot in the dark'; 'break the news'; 'in the long run' respectively.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom/phrase: 'all ears'
exp: 'all ears' means 'listening eagerly' (Hindi: पूरे ध्यान से सुनना). The other options are the meanings of 'at a premium'; 'a far cry'; 'an iron hand' respectively.

q:
Match the idioms in List-I with their meanings in List-II:
List-I: (A) Cry over spilt milk; (B) Leave no stone unturned; (C) All and sundry; (D) Dog in the manger
List-II: (1) to regret something that cannot be undone; (2) a person who neither uses a thing himself nor lets others use it; (3) everyone without distinction; (4) to make every possible effort
exp: Correct matching: 'cry over spilt milk' = to regret something that cannot be undone; 'leave no stone unturned' = to make every possible effort; 'all and sundry' = everyone without distinction; 'dog in the manger' = a person who neither uses a thing himself nor lets others use it. Hence A-1, B-4, C-3, D-2.

q: Choose the idiom/phrase that means: 'a wild guess'
exp: 'a shot in the dark' means 'a wild guess' (Hindi: अटकलबाज़ी, अंधेरे में तीर). Others: 'put one's foot down' = to take a firm stand; 'the talk of the town' = a person or thing everyone is talking about; 'bad blood' = ill feeling or enmity.

q: Which of the following idioms is NOT correctly matched with its meaning?
